title: SentinelEdge — On-Prem Security Runbook & Egress Sandboxing Session
summary: Redwood and SentinelEdge walked through on-prem/VPC network isolation, egress containment, KMS BYOK options, RBAC/SSO integration, and audit log retention. The customer stressed strict egress firewalling and HSM-backed keys. Agreed next steps: exchange network diagrams, run a short traffic-pattern benchmark, and share SOC 2/ISO artifacts and the private deployment runbook.
topics: On-prem deployment model and runner topology
transcript:
Meeting header: March 10, 2026 • 4:00 PM PDT • Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Rina Patel (Redwood Solutions), Priya Nair (SentinelEdge Head of Infra), Tom Blake (SentinelEdge Sec Eng), Alan Cho (CISO), Mei Wu (Network Lead)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we got about an hour, we'll go deep on the runbook and egress sandboxing. Quick intros then Diego will take us through the proposed on-prem topology.

[00:15] Priya Nair: Thanks Maya. Quick note from our side: timeline is Q2 pilot, production decision by Q3. Primary blockers are egress control and BYOK.

[00:32] Diego Alvarez: Great. I'll share my screen — apologies if the auto captions do weird stuff. So first slide, high-level: two deployment options we're seeing — private control plane with local runtime vs fully air-gapped on-prem. For SentinelEdge, given compliance you flagged, we recommend private control plane in a customer VPC that communicates over an mTLS channel and a local inference cluster with no public IPs.

[01:05] Tom Blake: When you say no public IPs, do you mean absolutely zero egress to internet or via a NAT with firewall rules? We need to ensure there's no uncontrolled egress to third-party telemetry.

[01:18] Rina Patel: We usually recommend zero direct outbound to the internet from the inference hosts. All outbound either goes through an egress gateway that you control (NGFW or proxy) or a queued NAT in a bastion-subnet with strict ACLs. We support explicit egress allow lists at the route/SG level.

[01:40] Mei Wu: For the egress gateway, we need DPI and logging. Can Redwood integrate with our existing Palo Alto tenant so we can inspect and drop non-whitelisted destinations?

[01:52] Diego Alvarez: Yes — nothing forces you to use Redwood-managed egress. The pattern we push is: inference nodes sit in private subnets; egress only via a controlled NAT/EGW that routes to your NGFW. We can also peer via PrivateLink for pulling model layers if you want to avoid internet.

[02:18] Alan Cho: On KMS — are we able to BYOK and use our HSM cluster? We can't have keys that can be exported to Redwood.

[02:30] Maya Chen: Short answer: yes, BYOK is supported. Long answer: we support customer-managed keys in your KMS (KMS/HSM) and mTLS for the key handshake. For on-prem we provide an HSM plugin that can be configured to use your HSM via an approved connector; keys never leave your HSM. We'll follow the BYOK onboarding checklist in the runbook.

[02:55] Tom Blake: Cool — need to confirm audited key access. We require that calls to decrypt are logged to a central SIEM and show user principal.

[03:05] Rina Patel: We emit key-use events with principal and request id; those can be forwarded to your SIEM over syslog or an observable collector. We also support forwarding detailed audit records to S3 in your account if you prefer object retention.

[03:28] Mei Wu: Retention question: regulator expects 7 years for some logs. What are our options for long-term storage?

[03:36] Diego Alvarez: You can configure audit log export to your storage with lifecycle policies. Redwood's default retention is 90 days in the control plane; for private you can push everything to your storage for arbitrary retention. There's also an option to stream to your Kafka or SIEM.

[03:56] Priya Nair: We also need to map RBAC to our existing roles — SRE, SecOps, AppEng, Auditor. Does Redwood support SCIM provisioning and role synchronization from Okta?

[04:10] Rina Patel: Yes — SAML SSO plus SCIM for user and group sync. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles. We support fine-grained RBAC: model-deployer, model-operator, viewer/auditor etc. We also have an auditor role that is read-only and can be scoped to token-level access for redaction.

[04:35] Tom Blake: A couple of nitty-gritty items: 1) we can't allow debug tokens or shell access to the model nodes without explicit JIT approval. 2) need session recordings for any admin sessions that access keys.

[04:48] Diego Alvarez: For JIT and privileged access we integrate with your existing PAM (just-in-time). For debug shells, our runbook includes a process that requires a signed approval and ephemeral creds; session recordings can be forwarded to your central recorder.

[05:12] Maya Chen: Ok I want to pause and underline the egress sandboxing scenario you mentioned in the invite. Diego, can you run through the sandbox flow?

[05:20] Diego Alvarez: Sure — here's the flow: create an isolated subnet for the inference pool with no outbound route; spin up a sandbox appliance that has a controlled outbound channel to your NGFW and a separate telemetry sink. The sandbox verifies model prompts for PII exfil patterns with a lightweight detector. If suspicious, traffic is quarantined to a holding queue for manual review. It's more of a policy layer we can attach, not baked into model logits.

[05:54] Priya Nair: That sounds promising — is the PII detector model local or cloud hosted? If cloud, that's a non-starter.

[06:03] Rina Patel: All detectors for this on-prem pattern run locally. The sandbox is a containerized microservice that performs regex and ML checks against a local ruleset. Nothing is sent to Redwood unless explicitly permitted by policy and a signed release.

[06:25] Tom Blake: About network egress — we need egress whitelists that are CIDR and FQDN based. Also, we want DNS-exfil protections — do you support DNS proxying or DoH blocking?

[06:38] Diego Alvarez: We can integrate with your DNS enforcement via a forwarder. Another pattern is to use a DNS proxy that resolves only approved names; any unknown resolution gets NXDOMAIN or goes to the sandbox. We can push DNS logs to the SIEM.

[06:58] Mei Wu: For multi-tenant logs we need token-level separation so audit entries always include tenant_id and model_version.

[07:08] Rina Patel: Audit schema includes tenant, principal, request_id, model_version, token_count, and outcome. CSV or JSON formats. Note sometimes auto transcriptions show K V cash — apologies, the captions can't help themselves.

[07:30] Alan Cho: On certifications — do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 artifacts we can review? We need the control matrix and the SRM.

[07:38] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll send the SOC 2 Type II report under NDA and the ISO statement of applicability. For private deployments we also provide the on-prem security checklist and the runbook with all controls mapped to the SOC/ISO control IDs.

[07:58] Tom Blake: Let's talk about network segmentation. We run a strict zero-trust overlay — no east-west traffic unless approved. How do Redwood nodes that need to share KV caches or model shards communicate?

[08:12] Diego Alvarez: Within the cluster we assume a segmented service mesh — we can integrate with your Istio/consul mesh. Traffic is mTLS between nodes, and node-to-node keys rotate frequently. If you can't allow internal mesh, we can enable a store-and-forward pattern with encrypted volumes and no direct traffic.

[08:35] Priya Nair: Performance trade-offs on the store-and-forward approach?

[08:41] Diego Alvarez: It adds some latency — anywhere from 10-60ms per call depending on your network. For production low-latency needs you probably want in-cluster mTLS. We can also run a dedicated NIC for model traffic to isolate it from other network traffic.

[09:02] Mei Wu: On firewalling: do we need to open ephemeral ports? Our policy forbids opening ephemeral ports in the DMZ.

[09:10] Rina Patel: We can design the control plane to use fixed ports and a single outbound allowed port on the egress gateway. The data plane model RPCs are internal only. When we require ephemeral ports for certain kernels or RPC layers we can tunnel them over a fixed port with an internal proxy.

[09:34] Tom Blake: Let's talk about pen tests and vulnerability scans — do you allow us to run authenticated scans against the deployment?

[09:42] Maya Chen: Yes, with bounds defined in the runbook. For private/on-prem deployments we expect customers to run periodic authenticated scans; we will provide contact windows and a staging environment. For host-level checks we provide a CVE list and a remediation timeline.

[09:59] Alan Cho: What about image provenance and SBOMs? We need attestations for the runtime images.

[10:07] Rina Patel: We publish SBOMs for the runtime and all dependencies. For on-prem we also supply signed attestations for each image and a recommended process for scanning before deployment.

[10:24] Priya Nair: Ok, wrapping into an example run: we want a pilot with 5 GPUs in a private subnet, no internet egress, log streaming to our SIEM, keys in our HSM, RBAC mapped to Okta groups, and a sandbox layer that holds outbound model outputs for DLP checks. Cost sensitivity moderate.

[10:44] Diego Alvarez: That pilot matches a common pattern. We'll propose a topology diagram and a checklist for the pilot. Also a small benchmark plan — synthetic traffic with your prompt set to measure tail latency with our batching and KV cache on.

[11:02] Tom Blake: On the benchmark: we want to ensure the KV cache isn't a risk — can cache entries be redacted or encrypted with tenant keys?

[11:12] Rina Patel: Cache at rest is encrypted with the node's disk encryption and the KMS-managed key. For stronger isolation we can encrypt per-tenant using tenant-specific keys stored in your KMS. Cache TTL policies can be short for sensitive workloads.

[11:36] Maya Chen: Great. I'm going to read out next steps and action items.

[11:40] Maya Chen: Next steps: 1) Redwood will send the private-deployment runbook, SOC 2 and ISO artifacts under NDA. 2) SentinelEdge to share the network diagram and a whitelist of mandatory NGFW controls. 3) Schedule the benchmark week (2 hours lab time + 1 tech sync). 4) Redwood to produce a pilot topology and cost estimate.

[11:58] Priya Nair: Sounds good — would like the runbook this week.

[12:02] Maya Chen: We'll send by end of week. Thanks everyone.

[12:06] Tom Blake: Thanks — appreciate the detail.

[12:12] (meeting ends)

SentinelEdge to share current network diagram, NGFW ruleset, and approved HSM vendor details (due: 2026-03-17)
Schedule 2-hour benchmark lab window and follow-up technical sync (owner: Diego Alvarez) (target week of 2026-03-23)
Redwood to provide pilot topology diagram and cost estimate for 5-GPU pilot (due: 2026-03-15)
